implementation_notes: Language-neutral discipline, in this order and no other: (1) PROFILE - produce the attribution that says where the time actually goes, at function or line granularity, and record it next to the code you are about to change. (2) BOUND - check the cost model before starting: the hotspot's share of the runtime caps the win (Amdahl), and an L1 hit (~1 ns) against a DRAM miss (~80 ns) decides whether memory or arithmetic dominates. (3) ONE CHANGE - apply a single targeted transformation at the hotspot: a layout change, an allocation removed, a branch removed, a call inlined. (4) VERIFY - a stable, warmed-up benchmark whose noise floor is smaller than the claimed win. (5) GUARD - keep that benchmark in CI so the win cannot rot. If you cannot do step 1, you are guessing - which is what the 97%/3% rule exists to prevent.
idiom_name: profile -> bound the opportunity (Amdahl + memory latency) -> one change -> verify on a stable benchmark -> keep the guard
code_sketch:
# The loop. In this order.
#
# 1. PROFILE. Record the attribution before editing. Knuth's finding is that
#    intuition-guided guesses about which code is hot fail - always measure.
#    profile -> 'processOrder: 62% of samples (cache misses), parseOrder: 4%'
#
# 2. BOUND. Amdahl: a hotspot that is 4% of the runtime caps the win at 4%,
#    however clever the change. Memory latency: L1 ~1ns, LLC ~40ns,
#    DRAM ~80ns, so a 5% miss rate costs ~4ns/op - more than the arithmetic.
#    => 'processOrder is 62%: optimise it. parseOrder at 4%: leave it alone.'
#
# 3. ONE CHANGE. Layout, allocation, branch, call, algorithm. One at a time,
#    so the before/after is attributable.
#    struct-of-arrays instead of array-of-pointers; hoist the allocation;
#    hoist the attribute lookup; swap the algorithm.
#
# 4. VERIFY. A stable, warmed-up benchmark whose NOISE FLOOR is below the
#    claimed win. If the run-to-run spread is 8%, a 5% 'win' is nothing.
#
# 5. GUARD. Keep the benchmark in CI with a threshold, so the win cannot rot.
#
# If step 1 is impossible, you are guessing - that is what the 97%/3% rule
# exists to prevent.
pitfalls: Optimising before profiling - the intuition-guided guess is wrong more often than right.
Optimising the 97% instead of the 3%; Amdahl caps the win at the hotspot's share.
One-shot timing with a cold cache or a cold JIT tier 'proving' a win that does not reproduce.
Several changes with one benchmark, so a regression cannot be attributed.
No regression guard, so the win rots silently as surrounding code changes.
